name: Buffer pH Calculator (Henderson–Hasselbalch)
seoDesc: The pH of a buffer depends on the ratio of its conjugate base to its acid, not on how concentrated it is: pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]). Free buffer ph (henders
summary:
The pH of a buffer depends on the ratio of its conjugate base to its acid, not on how concentrated it is: pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]). It returns base ÷ acid ratio, target pH, pH − pKa and acid share, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator gives the ratio for a target pH, the pH for a ratio you already have, and the ionic strength the mixture contributes. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Buffer pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch)
sections.html:
pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻] ÷ [HA]). Base share = 10^(pH−pKa) ÷ (1 + 10^(pH−pKa)) × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
pKanegative log of the acid dissociation constant—
[A⁻]concentration of the deprotonated formM
[HA]concentration of the protonated formM

sections.title: How do I use the Buffer pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch)?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the pKa of the buffer you are making (phosphate 7.2, HEPES 7.55, Tris 8.06).
  2. Enter the pH you need. The ratio and the share of each form follow.
  3. If you know the total concentration, the amount of acid and base form is filled in too.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: pka of the buffer of 7.2, total buffer concentration of 50 mM.

Substituting them into the formula gives base ÷ acid ratio of 1.58, target ph of 7.4 pH, ph − pka of 0.2 pH, acid share of 38.69%, base share of 61.31%, concentration of the acid form of 19.34 mM, concentration of the base form of 30.66 mM.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
pH = pKa50 / 50maximum buffer capacity, minimum pH drift on dilution
within ±1 of pKaUseful buffercapacity is still good
more than 1 unit awayPoor bufferalmost all of it is one form; pick another buffer

  • Buffer capacity is highest at pH = pKa, where the two forms are equal. A buffer is only worth using within about one pH unit of its pKa.

  • pKa depends on temperature: Tris drops about 0.03 pH units per °C, which is why a Tris buffer made at 25 °C reads about 7.8 in a cold room at 4 °C.

  • This equation ignores activity coefficients. At 100 mM and above, real pH drifts by a few tenths from the calculated value — measure it.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Confusing the ratio of the two forms with the ratio of stock volumes — a 1 M stock of each is the only case where they are the same.
  • Making a buffer at a pH far from the pKa and expecting it to hold.
  • Forgetting that adding HCl or NaOH changes the volume and therefore the final concentration.

faq.q: How much can I dilute a buffer before the pH changes?
faq.a: Dilution does not change the ratio, so pH holds; capacity falls, which matters once you add acid or base.

faq.q: Why is my measured pH different from the calculation?
faq.a: Temperature, ionic strength and activity coefficients all shift it; calibrate at the temperature you will use.

faq.q: What does the Buffer pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns base ÷ acid ratio, target pH, pH − pKa and acid share. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
